```java
// AuthenticationService.java:451 and :454 (replacement)
                char[] password = readPassword(options, "New password: ");   // no caller data in the prompt
                try {
                    service.register(address, password);
                    System.out.println("Registered " + displaySafe(address) + ".");
```

```java
// AuthenticationService.java (new helper next to wipe())
    /** Strips control characters from anything echoed back to an operator's terminal or log. */
    static String displaySafe(String value) {
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder(value.length());
        for (int i = 0; i < value.length(); i++) {
            char c = value.charAt(i);
            out.append(c < 0x20 || c == 0x7F ? ' ' : c);
        }
        return out.toString();
    }
```

### SEC-07: Redirected stdin materialises the password in an immutable `String`

**Severity:** Low
**CWE:** CWE-316: Cleartext Persistence of Sensitive Information in Memory
**Location:** `AuthenticationService.java:495`–`:496`

**Vulnerable code:**

```java
// AuthenticationService.java:487-497
    private static char[] readPassword(CliOptions options, String prompt) throws IOException {
        Console console = System.console();
        if (console != null) {
            char[] secret = console.readPassword(prompt);
            return secret == null ? new char[0] : secret;
        }
        System.out.print(prompt);
        System.out.flush();
        String line = options.input().readLine();
        return line == null ? new char[0] : line.toCharArray();
    }
```

**Why it is a problem:** The interactive branch is careful — `Console.readPassword` returns a
`char[]` that `authenticate()`/`register()` overwrite. The redirected branch is not: `readLine()`
returns an immutable `String`, which cannot be zeroed by any caller, and it is produced through a
`BufferedReader` (`:578`) that also holds the line in its internal `char[]` buffer. The `char[]`
handed to `register()` is a *copy* (`line.toCharArray()`), so wiping it — which `register()` does, per
SEC-05's fix — leaves the original characters intact in the `String` and in the reader's buffer,
where they stay reachable until collection and may land in a swap file or a heap dump. The javadoc
above `readPassword` reasons correctly about not trimming a trailing space and concludes "there is
nothing to hide it from" when input is redirected; that is true of *shoulder surfing* but not of
*memory residue*, which is the residue the rest of the file works to remove.

**Fix:** Read the redirected line as bytes and build the `char[]` directly, clearing the scratch
buffer, and read line-at-a-time rather than through a buffering reader for the secret.

```java
// AuthenticationService.java:495-496 (replacement)
        System.out.print(prompt);
        System.out.flush();
        return readRawLine(options.inputStream());   // byte-wise; no String, no BufferedReader
    }

    /** Reads one line into a char[] with no intermediate String or read-ahead buffer. */
    static char[] readRawLine(InputStream in) throws IOException {
        char[] buf = new char[1025];
        int n = 0;
        int c;
        while ((c = in.read()) != -1 && c != '\n') {
            if (n < buf.length - 1) {
                buf[n++] = (char) (c & 0xFF);
            }
        }
        char[] out = Arrays.copyOf(buf, n);
        Arrays.fill(buf, (char) 0);
        return out;
    }
```

### SEC-08: `add-user` discloses whether an account exists

**Severity:** Low
**CWE:** CWE-204: Observable Response Discrepancy
**Location:** `AuthenticationService.java:454` (contrasting branch at `:459`–`:462`)

**Vulnerable code:**

```java
// AuthenticationService.java:452-462
                try {
                    service.register(address, password);
                    System.out.println("Registered " + address + ".");
                } catch (InvalidInputException bad) {
                    System.out.println(bad.getMessage());
                    System.exit(2);
                    return;
                } catch (SQLException taken) {
                    // Driver text can echo the statement, so only the class is reported.
                    System.out.println("Could not register that email address ("
                            + taken.getClass().getSimpleName() + ").");
```

**Why it is a problem:** A successful insert prints `Registered <addr>.` while a violation of
`CONSTRAINT users_email_unique` (schema.sql) prints `Could not register that email address
(SQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException).`, and the process exit code differs (0 versus 1). Any
caller of `add-user` can therefore enumerate which addresses already have accounts, one line of output
per probe. The design elsewhere goes out of its way to close exactly this channel on the login path —
`DUMMY_HASH` at `:53` burns a full digest so "no such account" is not measurably faster, and denial
text is identical for unknown account and wrong password — so the registration path is the one place
the oracle reopens. Severity is Low rather than Medium because reaching this path requires the
database write credentials that `--jdbc`/`--user`/`DB_PASSWORD` supply (`:444`, `:564`), and anyone
holding those can query the table directly; the realistic exposure is a wrapper that exposes
`add-user` more widely than it exposes the database.

**Fix:** Print one indistinguishable line for both outcomes and reserve the distinction for an
operator-only diagnostic switch.

```java
// AuthenticationService.java:452-463 (replacement)
                try {
                    service.register(address, password);
                    System.exit(0);
                } catch (InvalidInputException bad) {
                    System.out.println(bad.getMessage());
                    System.exit(2);
                    return;
                } catch (SQLException taken) {
                    // Same text and same exit code as success: this path must not confirm
                    // that the address already has an account.
                    System.out.println("Registration request processed for " + displaySafe(address) + ".");
                    System.exit(0);
                }
                System.out.println("Registration request processed for " + displaySafe(address) + ".");
```

(If scripts genuinely need to know whether the insert happened, gate that behind an explicit
`--report-duplicates` flag that is off by default and documented as an enumeration channel.)

### SEC-09: Non-interactive login requires the password in a plaintext file

**Severity:** Low
**CWE:** CWE-313: Cleartext Storage in a File or on Disk (with CWE-772: Missing Release of Resource)
**Location:** `AuthenticationService.java:575`–`:577` (option declared at `:521`, parsed at `:539`)

**Vulnerable code:**

```java
// AuthenticationService.java:574-578
    BufferedReader input() throws IOException {
        InputStream source = stdinFile != null
                ? new FileInputStream(stdinFile)
                : System.in;
        input = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(source, StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
```

```java
// AuthH2Test.java:357
        Files.write(stdinFile, (ALICE + "\n" + ALICE_PW + "\n").getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
```

**Why it is a problem:** `--stdin-file` is the documented way to log in without a terminal, so using
it at all means putting the account password into an ordinary file — created with the process umask's
default permissions (typically world-readable, `0644`) and left on disk afterwards, as the suite
itself demonstrates at `AuthH2Test.java:357`. Any local user, any backup job, and any container image
layer that captures that path now holds a credential, which is exactly the exposure `Console`-based
prompting and `DB_PASSWORD`-only handling exist to avoid — the design is careful about not putting the
*database* password on the command line (`README.md:69`) while offering a flag that puts the *account*
password on disk. The file is also chosen by path with no restriction, so a wrapper that forwards a
caller-controlled value here turns the CLI into an arbitrary-file reader (its contents are not echoed,
but the login result becomes an oracle on file contents). Separately, the `BufferedReader` cached at
`:583` is never closed, so the descriptor stays open for the process lifetime — harmless for a
short-lived CLI, a leak for anything that embeds this class.

**Fix:** Prefer a descriptor or environment source for non-interactive use; if a file must be kept,
require tight permissions, refuse to proceed without them, and close the reader.

```java
// AuthenticationService.java:574-579 (replacement)
    BufferedReader input() throws IOException {
        InputStream source;
        if (stdinFile != null) {
            Path p = Path.of(stdinFile);
            if (!Files.getPosixFilePermissions(p).equals(
                    Set.of(PosixFilePermission.OWNER_READ, PosixFilePermission.OWNER_WRITE))) {
                throw new IOException(stdinFile + " must be mode 600 to be used as an input file");
            }
            source = new FileInputStream(p.toFile());
        } else {
            source = System.in;
        }
        input = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(source, StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        return input;
    }

    void closeInput() throws IOException {
        if (input != null) {
            input.close();
            input = null;
        }
    }
```

## 6. Verified Controls and Checks With No Finding

- **SQL injection (`AuthenticationService.java`)** — reviewed with
  `exploiting-sql-injection-vulnerabilities`. Both statements are `static final` compile-time
  constants (`:34`, `:37`); the predicate is a single equality with no `LIKE`, `IN`, `ORDER BY` or
  identifier position that could need concatenation; both values are bound with `setString`
  (`:111`, `:144`–`:145`); there is no `createStatement` anywhere in the service, so there is no path
  that accepts raw text; `setQueryTimeout(5)` (`:110`, `:143`) bounds slow injected work; only the
  first row is consumed. `AuthDoublesTest` records statement text to prove the address never appears
  in it, and the CLI test at `AuthH2Test.java:389` runs `--email "x' OR '1'='1"` against the real
  database and expects refusal. The service's own `README.md:122` correctly notes there is no
  `Statement.execute` path that would accept two semicolon-separated statements. **No finding.**
- **Deliberate concatenation in the test suite** (`AuthH2Test.java:184`–`:194`) — `vulnerableLookup`
  does build SQL by `+` and calls `createStatement`, but it exists only to prove the injection test
  would fail if the service ever regressed (a positive control); it is never reachable from
  `AuthenticationService`. **No finding**, and it should not be removed.
- **Error-based information leakage** — `SQLException` text and stack traces are never printed:
  `:85`–`:86` and `:461`–`:462` print `getClass().getSimpleName()` only, with the comment at `:460`
  recording why. Login denial text is uniform, and `AuthH2Test.java:318`–`:319` asserts the password
  is never echoed back. **No finding.**
- **Password hashing and comparison** — reviewed with `performing-cryptographic-audit-of-application`.
  `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256` (`:336`), 16-byte salt from `SecureRandom` (`:338`, `:349`), 32-byte digest
  (`:339`), 100 000 rounds for new records (`:337`), format is self-describing so parameters travel
  with the record, `salt.length` and `expected.length` and a maximum round count are all validated
  before use (`:379`–`:381`), and comparison uses `MessageDigest.isEqual` (`:388`) rather than
  `Arrays.equals`/`String.equals`. `PBEKeySpec` cannot encode NUL or unpaired surrogates, and
  `requireUsablePassword` rejects exactly those characters (`:236`–`:248`) so two different inputs
  cannot digest identically. **No finding** (the accepted-round floor is SEC-03).
- **Timing-based account enumeration** — a missing row returns `DUMMY_HASH` (`:114`, `:117`) built at
  class load from a random salt and the real round count (`:252`–`:262`), and a malformed stored
  record triggers `digestQuietly` (`:365`, `:376`, `:382`, `:400`–`:404`) so a rejected answer costs
  the same as a verified one. `DUMMY_SALT` (`:408`) and the `System.nanoTime()` filler (`:256`) are
  padding material, not secrets — the security property is that the *salt is random and the work is
  real*, both of which hold. **No finding.**
- **Fail-open on infrastructure error** — a `SQLException` (`:83`–`:88`) or an unverifiable stored
  record (`:93`–`:98`) returns `AuthResult.unavailable()` and never `success()`; `buildDummyHash()`
  turns a missing PBKDF2 implementation into `ExceptionInInitializerError` (`:263`–`:266`) so the
  class refuses to load rather than accept logins. **No finding.**
- **Credential storage and CLI secret handling** — reviewed with
  `implementing-secret-scanning-with-gitleaks`'s checklist. Only the digest is stored
  (`schema.sql`, `INSERT_USER`); `DB_PASSWORD` is read from the environment (`:564`–`:566`) with no
  default leaked; a `--password` flag is refused as `Unknown argument:` (`:545`), which `README.md:69`
  documents as intentional. Literal secrets are limited to documented test fixtures
  (`AuthH2Test.java:41`, `:43`, `:214`) chosen to share no substring so an echo test cannot pass by
  accident (`README.md:345`). No key, token, or production credential anywhere in the folder,
  including `return.txt`. **No finding.**
- **SSRF** — checked with `exploiting-server-side-request-forgery`; the program performs no URL or HTTP
  fetch and resolves no caller-supplied host. The only URL-shaped input is the operator-supplied
  `--jdbc` value used at `:444`, which is an operator-trusted connection string, not attacker data, and
  `README.md:210` correctly makes TLS that connection's responsibility. **No matching behaviour, so no
  finding.**
- **Session management** — out of scope by design and correctly so: `authenticate()` returns a
  yes/no answer and mints no token or cookie (`README.md:202`). There is no session artifact to
  mis-issue. **No finding.**
- **Mutation battery as evidence** — `run-mutation-battery.py` includes `sql-raw-concat`,
  `register-email-concat`, `iterations-set-to-one`, `round-count-floor-lowered-to-100`,
  `digest-arrays-equals`, `stored-digest-logged-on-refusal` and `query-text-logged-with-value` among
  its 30 mutants, confirming the authors already treat those as security invariants the suites must
  catch. Its four `EQUIVALENT` survivors are argued, not silently accepted. This is a positive signal;
  note that `round-count-floor-lowered-to-100` being a *surviving-or-argued* case is consistent with
  SEC-03 — the floor's exact value is not pinned by any test.


---

### 43) results-cyber/qwen/qwen/set_a/sallie/4/basic/security_review.md

# Security Review: `account` — Java command-line registration and login program

## 1. Executive Summary

The component is a self-contained Java 17 command-line program that registers accounts and
authenticates them against a plain text file. Its cryptographic core is sound: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256
at 210,000 iterations, a fresh 16-byte `SecureRandom` salt per account, a 256-bit digest compared in
constant time, plus a set of deliberate hardenings (timing equalisation for unknown users, rejection
of passwords that `PBEKeySpec` cannot represent one-to-one, an allowlisted username charset,
fail-closed parsing of the store, and a locked read-modify-write with an atomic replace). The
widely abused classes of vulnerability are simply absent: there is no database, no HTML or template
output, no network I/O, no deserialisation of untrusted bytes, no subprocess, and no authorisation
boundary.

**Six findings: 0 Critical, 0 High, 2 Medium, 4 Low.** Both Mediums concern secret handling and
guess rate rather than broken cryptography — authentication is not throttled at all, and the
`verify` subcommand takes the password as a command-line argument where every local user can read
it. The Lows are a KDF-cost downgrade window that contradicts a documented guarantee, a password
copy that cannot be erased from memory on the piped input path, unvalidated text written to the
terminal and to captured logs, and a length-only password policy.

Two candidate findings were investigated and **disproved** rather than reported (see §6): the
store file does *not* inherit permissive permissions (`Files.createTempFile` creates it `0600` and
`ATOMIC_MOVE` is a rename that preserves those bits), and the prebuilt `out/account/*.class` files
that `run.sh` actually executes were disassembled with `javap` and match the reviewed sources in
every security-relevant constant and message. `README.md` already acknowledges several of the
accepted risks; where a risk is inherent to the design (the store file is not encrypted, usernames
are case-sensitive) it is not re-reported as a finding, but the missing throttling in SEC-01 is
reported despite being acknowledged, because it is the mechanism that turns a stolen store file into
a live guessing oracle.

## 2. Scope

| File | Purpose | Security-relevant behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src/account/Main.java` | CLI front end: parses argv, prompts, prints messages, sets exit codes | Accepts the store path and an arbitrary `verify` password from argv; reads secrets via `Console.readPassword` when available, otherwise via a piped line reader that returns a `String`; echoes unvalidated text (unknown command, store path) to stdout/stderr; prints exception messages only, never stack traces |
| `src/account/AccountService.java` | Registration and authentication use case | Allowlists usernames to `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` (3–32); burns equivalent key-derivation work for unknown users; returns distinct `UNKNOWN_USER` / `INVALID_CREDENTIALS` / `USERNAME_TAKEN` results; performs no attempt counting |
| `src/account/PasswordHasher.java` | Password hashing and verification | PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, 210 000 iterations, 16-byte `SecureRandom` salt, 256-bit output; constant-time comparison; trusts the iteration count stored in the file down to a 10 000 floor; length-only password policy |
| `src/account/AccountStore.java` | File-backed account registry | POSIX shared/exclusive `FileChannel` locking; re-read and merge under the exclusive lock; temp file + `ATOMIC_MOVE` replace; refuses corrupt or duplicated store files |
| `src/account/User.java` | One account and its one-line serialisation | Splits store lines on `\|`, fails closed on malformed records and bad timestamps; plaintext password never present |
| `src/test/account/AccountSystemTest.java` | 94-check self-test that drives the real program in a second process | Proves the collision guard, timing equalisation, and concurrent-registration behaviour; covers only a 1-iteration weakened record |
| `run.sh` | Builds if needed, then runs the program | Decides whether to rebuild by comparing the newest source against one class file's mtime; aborts on `javac` failure; `exec java -cp out account.Main "$@"` |
| `out/account/*.class`, `out-test/account/*.class` | Shipped bytecode that `run.sh` actually executes | Verified with `javap` to match `src/`; executed without a rebuild when sources are not strictly newer |
| `README.md` | Design and accepted-risk documentation | Not executable; used to distinguish deliberate choices from defects and to check documented guarantees against the code |

Not in scope as code: `prompt.txt`, `cyber_prompt.txt`, `prompt_hash.txt`, `result.md`, `return.txt`
(harness files, no executable content).

## 3. Skills Applied

- **`review-code-for-security-vulnerabilities`** — the dispatcher. Used for the whole engagement:
  established what each file does before judging it, then dispatched to the specialised skills below
  rather than pattern-matching on keywords. Its verification checklist (list the skills applied, give
  a CWE id and `file:line` for every finding) shapes this report.
- **`performing-cryptographic-audit-of-application`** — applied to `src/account/PasswordHasher.java`
  and its call sites: reviewed the primitive choice and parameters (algorithm, iteration count, key
  length), the source and uniqueness of the salt, the comparison function for early-exit leakage, key
  destruction after use, and the self-describing record format as a trust boundary. This skill's
  "Weak KDF / low iteration count" and "timing side-channel" rows drove SEC-03 and the two
  crypto controls recorded in §6.
- **`testing-api-authentication-weaknesses`** — applied to `AccountService.register`/`authenticate`
  and `Main.exitForLogin`/`exitForVerify`/`exitForRegister`: credential storage strength, absence of a
  session mechanism, response and timing discrepancies usable for account enumeration, and
  brute-force/lockout posture. Drove SEC-01 and SEC-06, and the enumeration controls in §6.
- **`testing-for-sensitive-data-exposure`** — applied to the credential store and all output paths:
  what the store file contains, the permissions of the store and its temp file, secrets in process
  arguments and echoed input, source-level scanning for embedded credentials, and whether error
  messages leak internal detail. Drove SEC-02, SEC-04 and SEC-05.
- **`exploiting-insecure-deserialization`** — applied to the store-parsing path (`User.fromLine`,
  `PasswordHasher.matches`, Base64 decoding) to check for unsafe object or type-driven parsing.
  No `ObjectInputStream`, no reflective type resolution, no gadget surface; parsing is length- and
  charset-checked and fails closed. No finding (§6).
- **`exploiting-race-condition-vulnerabilities`** — applied to `AccountStore.load`/`add`/`writeCurrent`
  for time-of-check/time-of-use between the in-memory snapshot, the duplicate-name check, and the file
  write. The critical section re-reads under an exclusive lock and replaces the file atomically, so
  concurrent registration loses no accounts and cannot smuggle a duplicate identity. No finding (§6).
- **`implementing-secret-scanning-with-gitleaks`** — its description matched the
  "secrets in source" question; not applied as a scanner because the repository is nine text files
  reviewed in full, so the equivalent check was done by reading. Only `EQUALIZING_PASSWORD` /
  `EQUALIZING_SALT` (`PasswordHasher.java:42-43`) look credential-like and they are timing pads, not
  secrets — deliberately **not** reported as CWE-798.

Reviewed against general OWASP Top 10 / CWE knowledge, because the library has no skill covering
the behaviour:

- **Authentication throttling and lockout** (`CWE-307`) — no skill in the library addresses
  rate limiting; SEC-01.
- **Secrets in process arguments and in non-zeroizable memory** (`CWE-522`, `CWE-316`) — SEC-02,
  SEC-04.
- **Output neutralisation for logs and terminals** (`CWE-117`) — control characters in the `--store`
  path and unknown-command text; SEC-05.
- **Password policy** (`CWE-521`) — SEC-06.
- **File and temporary-file permissions** (`CWE-732`, `CWE-377`) — checked and disproved (§6).
- **Shell command injection in `run.sh`** (`CWE-78`) — checked, no finding (§6); the library has no
  shell-injection skill.
- **Build-artifact integrity** — checked `out/account/*.class` against `src/` with `javap`, no
  finding (§6).
- **Broken access control** — not applicable: single-user local tool, one trust domain, no privilege
  or tenant boundary to cross. SQL injection, XSS, SSRF, XXE, path traversal and JWT findings are not
  applicable because no such surface exists (§6).

## 4. Summary of Findings

| ID | Title | Severity | CWE | Location |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SEC-01 | No limit on authentication attempts: no rate limiting, lockout, or backoff | Medium | CWE-307 | `src/account/AccountService.java:100-115` |
| SEC-02 | `verify` takes the password as a command-line argument, readable by any local user | Medium | CWE-522 | `src/account/Main.java:109-114` |
| SEC-03 | Stored PBKDF2 cost is trusted down to 10 000 iterations (21× below policy) | Low | CWE-916 | `src/account/PasswordHasher.java:27, 120-125` |
| SEC-04 | Password kept in an immutable, un-wipeable `String` on the piped input path | Low | CWE-316 | `src/account/Main.java:205-212` |
| SEC-05 | Unvalidated store path and command text written to the terminal and to logs | Low | CWE-117 | `src/account/Main.java:124-127` |
| SEC-06 | Password policy is length-only: no common-password or username containment screen | Low | CWE-521 | `src/account/PasswordHasher.java:55-64` |

## 5. Detailed Findings

### SEC-01: No limit on authentication attempts: no rate limiting, lockout, or backoff

- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
- **Location:** `src/account/AccountService.java:100-115`

**Vulnerable code:**

```java
// src/account/AccountService.java:100-115
    Result authenticate(String username, char[] password) {
        String name = normalizeUsername(username);
        try {
            PasswordHasher.validatePassword(password);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            return Result.INVALID_CREDENTIALS;
        }
        Optional<User> user = store.find(name);
        if (user.isEmpty()) {
            PasswordHasher.burnEquivalentWork();
            return Result.UNKNOWN_USER;
        }
        return PasswordHasher.matches(password, user.get().passwordEncoding())
                ? Result.AUTHENTICATED
                : Result.INVALID_CREDENTIALS;
    }
```

**Why it is a problem:** `authenticate` keeps no record that an attempt happened, and neither
`Main.exitForLogin` (`Main.java:91-107`) nor `Main.exitForVerify` (`Main.java:109-122`) adds one, so
every failure is followed immediately by permission to try again. `README.md` lists "rate limiting on
failed attempts, account lockout" under "What this program does not do", but the consequence is
concrete for this design: the whole defence in depth of the store is a per-guess cost of roughly a
third of a second, and there is exactly one such layer. Anyone able to invoke the program — a second
local user, a shared CI runner, a script that takes a username argument — can loop
`verify <user> <password>` over a dictionary indefinitely with no increasing cost, no lockout, and no
audit record of the attempt, so a slow-but-steady online guess against one account is invisible after
the fact. The 210 000 iterations make each guess expensive, not the attempt count bounded, and the
"unknown username" path costs a full derivation (`AccountService.java:107-111`), which means an
attacker spraying a username list pays the same price as an attacker guessing one account's password
and is equally unthrottled.

**Fix:** Record failures per username in a sidecar file and make the next attempt pay for them,
resetting on success. A per-username counter alone lets an attacker spray many names, so also cap
total failures across the store in the same window, and prefer a growing delay over a permanent
lockout so the throttle cannot itself disable an account.

```java
    Result authenticate(String username, char[] password) {
        String name = normalizeUsername(username);
        attempts.enforceDelay();          // sleeps on recent failures; throws if saturated
        try {
            PasswordHasher.validatePassword(password);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            attempts.recordFailure(name);
            return Result.INVALID_CREDENTIALS;
        }
        Optional<User> user = store.find(name);
        if (user.isEmpty()) {
            PasswordHasher.burnEquivalentWork();
            attempts.recordFailure(name);
            return Result.UNKNOWN_USER;
        }
        boolean ok = PasswordHasher.matches(password, user.get().passwordEncoding());
        if (ok) {
            attempts.clear(name);
        } else {
            attempts.recordFailure(name);
        }
        return ok ? Result.AUTHENTICATED : Result.INVALID_CREDENTIALS;
    }
```

`AttemptTracker.enforceDelay()` should read a store-sidecar file written under the same exclusive
lock used by `AccountStore.add`, sleep `min(cap, base * 2^failures)` once the count in the current
window exceeds a small threshold, and count failures globally as well as per username; because the
counter file lives beside the store, a reset requires write access to the store itself.

### SEC-02: `verify` takes the password as a command-line argument, readable by any local user

- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-522: Insufficiently Protected Credentials
- **Location:** `src/account/Main.java:109-114`

**Vulnerable code:**

```java
// src/account/Main.java:109-114
    private static void exitForVerify(AccountService service, String[] operands) {
        if (operands.length != 2) {
            ERR.println("Error: verify needs a username and a password.");
            System.exit(2);
        }
        char[] password = operands[1].toCharArray();
```

**Why it is a problem:** Command-line arguments are world-readable on Linux through
`/proc/<pid>/cmdline` (mode `0444`), so for the lifetime of the JVM any user on the machine can read
the plaintext password with a plain `ps -ef` or by watching `/proc`; the same string is then retained
in shell history, in `ps`-based monitoring and process-accounting data, and in CI job logs. The
program's own help text acknowledges this at `Main.java:136-137` ("Same check with the password on the
command line (for scripts only - it is visible to other processes)") and `README.md` repeats it, but
documenting an exposure does not narrow it, and the recommendation targets scripts — the exact context
in which the credential ends up committed to a repository or echoed into a build log. This is also the
only path that bypasses the careful secret handling everywhere else: `register` and `login` prompt via
`Console.readPassword` and never put the secret in argv, and `exitForVerify` still zeroes the buffer
(`Main.java:120`), which cannot help once the value was transmitted in the clear. (Also commonly
reported as the "sensitive information in a command-line argument" exposure, CWE-214.)

**Fix:** Take only the username as an operand and read the secret from a channel that is not world
readable — stdin, or an environment variable, whose `/proc/<pid>/environ` is owner-read-only — while
keeping the interactive prompt as the default:

```java
    private static void exitForVerify(AccountService service, String[] operands) {
        if (operands.length != 1) {
            ERR.println("Error: verify needs a username; the password comes from stdin"
                    + " or $ACCOUNT_PASSWORD, never from the command line.");
            System.exit(2);
        }
        String fromEnv = System.getenv("ACCOUNT_PASSWORD");
        char[] password = fromEnv != null ? fromEnv.toCharArray() : readSecret("Password: ", true);
        try {
            AccountService.Result result = service.authenticate(operands[0], password);
            OUT.println(result == AccountService.Result.AUTHENTICATED ? "OK" : "FAIL");
            System.exit(result == AccountService.Result.AUTHENTICATED ? 0 : 1);
        } finally {
            Arrays.fill(password, (char) 0);
        }
    }
```

If a two-operand call must keep working for one release, reject it unless an explicit
`--allow-password-in-argv` flag is present, and print a warning to stderr on that path so the
exposure is never silent.

### SEC-03: Stored PBKDF2 cost is trusted down to 10 000 iterations (21× below policy)

- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-916: Use of Password Hash With Insufficient Computational Effort
- **Location:** `src/account/PasswordHasher.java:27, 120-125`

**Vulnerable code:**

```java
// src/account/PasswordHasher.java:27
    private static final int MIN_ITERATIONS = 10_000;
// ... (lines 28-119 elided)
// src/account/PasswordHasher.java:120-125
        // A stored record is only trusted if its cost is still sane: otherwise a
        // tampered file could ask for one iteration and make cracking cheap.
        if (iterations < MIN_ITERATIONS || iterations > MAX_ITERATIONS
                || salt.length < SALT_BYTES || expected.length != HASH_BITS / 8) {
            return false;
        }
```

**Why it is a problem:** The iteration count travels inside the stored record, and the only floor
applied to it at verification time is `MIN_ITERATIONS = 10_000` — 21× cheaper than the `ITERATIONS =
210_000` the program itself writes. Rewriting one field of one record from `$210000$` to `$10000$`
leaves the account fully functional while making its hash 21 times cheaper to attack, and it does so
without any other observable change; the same holds for any old, cheap record restored from a backup.
This contradicts a guarantee `README.md` states outright ("A weakened record in the file is not
trusted. If somebody edits a stored record to say 'one round of maths', logging in with the matching
password is still refused") — a record claiming one round *is* refused, but the accepted range reaches
a tenth of the policy cost, and `AccountSystemTest.weakStoredCostIsRejected()`
(`src/test/account/AccountSystemTest.java:303-309`) only exercises the single case
`pbkdf2-sha256$1$...`, so the downgrade in the 10 000–209 999 band is neither blocked nor tested. The
severity is Low rather than higher because exploiting it needs write access to the store file, and an
attacker with that access can already run guesses offline against the original record — the damage is
a silent weakening of the one remaining defence, not a new entry path.

**Fix:** Separate the compatibility floor from the policy floor, and refuse anything below policy
instead of below "not absurd". Raising a legacy record is a re-hash on successful login, not a
refusal:

```java
    static final int ITERATIONS = 210_000;
    // Cost a stored record may claim: anything below the current policy is a downgrade,
    // not a legacy record, because re-stretching happens on a successful login.
    private static final int MIN_ACCEPTED_ITERATIONS = 100_000;

        if (iterations < MIN_ACCEPTED_ITERATIONS || iterations > MAX_ITERATIONS
                || salt.length < SALT_BYTES || expected.length != HASH_BITS / 8) {
            return false;
        }
```

Then have the successful-login path re-write the record with `hash(password)` at `ITERATIONS` so
records at the policy floor are pulled back up to 210 000 rather than being tolerated indefinitely.

### SEC-04: Password kept in an immutable, un-wipeable `String` on the piped input path

- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-316: Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information in Memory
- **Location:** `src/account/Main.java:205-212`

**Vulnerable code:**

```java
// src/account/Main.java:205-212
        if (warnIfEchoed) {
            ERR.println("Note: no console attached, the password will be echoed as you type it.");
        }
        String value = promptLine(prompt);
        if (value.isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("a password is required");
        }
        return value.toCharArray();
```

**Why it is a problem:** When no console is attached, the secret is read as a `String`
(`promptLine`, `Main.java:164-189`) and only then copied into a `char[]`. Every later zeroing — the
`Arrays.fill(password, (char) 0)` in `exitForRegister`/`exitForLogin`/`exitForVerify` — wipes the
*copy*, while the original `String` stays intact and un-wipeable in the heap until the garbage
collector moves or frees it, and `String` contents may additionally survive in the `BufferedReader`
line buffer that produced it. That defeats the reason the rest of the program uses `char[]` and
`Console.readPassword` at all: on this path a core dump, a heap dump taken for another purpose, or a
debugger attached to the process yields the password directly. The same fallback has a second,
smaller inconsistency: the echo warning is printed only when `warnIfEchoed` is true, and
`exitForLogin` passes `false` (`Main.java:93`), so under `script(1)` or a pseudo-terminal without a
Java console the login password is displayed with no notice at all — the "said out loud rather than
hidden" promise in the class comment holds for registration but not for login.

**Fix:** Read the line straight into a growable `char[]` so no `String` copy of the secret is ever
created, and warn on every no-console path rather than only on registration:

```java
    private static char[] readSecret(String prompt, boolean warnIfEchoed) {
        Console console = System.console();
        if (console != null) {
            char[] secret = console.readPassword("%s", prompt);
            if (secret == null || secret.length == 0) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("a password is required");
            }
            return secret;
        }
        ERR.println("Note: no console attached - the password is not hidden and cannot be"
                + " erased from memory; run from a terminal to avoid this.");
        return readSecretFromPipe(prompt);   // fills a char[], returns an exact-length copy,
    }                                        // zeroing the scratch buffer in a finally block
```

A `readSecretFromPipe` implementation should `Reader.read(char[], int, 1)` characters from
`new InputStreamReader(System.in, UTF_8)` into a scratch `char[]` until `'\n'`, return an exact-length
copy, and zero the scratch buffer in a `finally` block.

### SEC-05: Unvalidated store path and command text written to the terminal and to logs

- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-117: Improper Output Neutralization for Logs
- **Location:** `src/account/Main.java:124-127`

**Vulnerable code:**

```java
// src/account/Main.java:124-127
    private static void exitForList(AccountService service) {
        OUT.println(service.accountCount() + " account(s) stored in " + service.storeFile());
        System.exit(0);
    }
```

**Why it is a problem:** The store path is never validated — `AccountStore` only absolutises and
normalises it (`AccountStore.java:36`), which does not remove control characters — and it is
interpolated verbatim into program output here and at `Main.java:79-80`. The first argv element is
echoed the same way for an unrecognised command (`Main.java:50`). Two consequences follow. CR or LF
inside the path or command forges additional output lines, so when stdout or stderr is collected into
a log — the normal deployment for a scripted credential check — an attacker who influences those
arguments can fabricate entries that appear to come from this program, for example a second
"account(s) stored in" line naming a file that was never touched. ESC and OSC sequences survive to the
terminal and are interpreted there: `OSC 52` sets the clipboard, `OSC 8` inserts a clickable hyperlink
with arbitrary label and target, `OSC 0`/`OSC 2` rewrite the window title, so the output of a command
whose arguments came from elsewhere (a wrapper script, a filename, a CI matrix entry) can plant a
misleading line plus a link whose label is not its destination. This is an inconsistency rather than an
unknown risk class in this codebase: the username is allowlisted to `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` precisely to stop
invisible characters from reaching stored or displayed identities, yet the path and command bypass all
screening. Note also that the success message prints `username.trim()` — the raw argument — rather
than the validated value; it is safe today only because `register` throws first for any character
outside the allowlist, an ordering dependency that will silently break if the message is ever reached
by another path.

**Fix:** Neutralise control characters on every path that echoes data the program did not construct,
and print the validated username rather than the raw argument:

```java
    private static String safeDisplay(String value) {
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder(value.length());
        for (int i = 0; i < value.length(); i++) {
            char c = value.charAt(i);
            if (c < 0x20 || c == 0x7f) {
                out.append(String.format("\\u%04x", (int) c));   // CR, LF, ESC, DEL neutralised
            } else {
                out.append(c);
            }
        }
        return out.toString();
    }

    private static void exitForList(AccountService service) {
        OUT.println(service.accountCount() + " account(s) stored in "
                + safeDisplay(service.storeFile().toString()));
        System.exit(0);
    }
```

Apply the same helper at `Main.java:50` (`safeDisplay(command)`) and `Main.java:79-80`, and use the
value returned by `AccountService.normalizeUsername` for the registered-username message.

### SEC-06: Password policy is length-only: no common-password or username containment screen

- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-521: Weak Password Requirements
- **Location:** `src/account/PasswordHasher.java:55-64`

**Vulnerable code:**

```java
// src/account/PasswordHasher.java:55-64
    static void validatePassword(char[] password) {
        if (password == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("password is missing");
        }
        if (password.length < MIN_PASSWORD_CHARS) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("password must be at least " + MIN_PASSWORD_CHARS + " characters");
        }
        if (password.length > MAX_PASSWORD_CHARS) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("password must be at most " + MAX_PASSWORD_CHARS + " characters");
        }
```

**Why it is a problem:** The remaining checks in this method (`PasswordHasher.java:65-79`) exist only
to reject passwords `PBEKeySpec` cannot represent one-to-one, so the *policy* is exactly "at least 10
characters" — `password1234`, `1234567890` and `qwertyuiop` are all accepted. The store file keeps no
secret of its own, so the work factor protects only against guesses a dictionary will never reach; a
ten-character common word is recovered in a fraction of the guesses the 210 000 iterations are there
to make expensive, which means the KDF budget is spent protecting the passwords least worth
protecting. There is also no relation check between the two inputs the user supplies in the same
command: `./run.sh register alice` followed by the password `alice123456` is accepted, and the
username sits in plaintext on the same line as the record, so it is the first thing a guesser tries.
This is not a case of missing code the project declined to write — `validatePassword` is the designed
enforcement point and is already called from both `register` and `authenticate`
(`AccountService.java:84, 103`) — but it is Low because the exposure requires the store file to be
read, and per-account salts prevent one cracked password from being replayed against the others.

**Fix:** Screen against a built-in list of the most common leaked passwords and against the username,
keeping the representability checks as they are:

```java
    private static final Set<String> FORBIDDEN = CommonPasswords.topTenThousand();

    static void validatePassword(String username, char[] password) {
        // ... existing null, length, NUL and surrogate checks unchanged ...
        char[] lowered = Character.toLowerCase(password[0]) == password[0]
                ? password : java.util.Arrays.copyOf(password, password.length);
        for (int i = 0; i < lowered.length; i++) {
            lowered[i] = Character.toLowerCase(lowered[i]);
        }
        boolean forbidden = FORBIDDEN.contains(new String(lowered))
                || (username != null && containsIgnoreCase(lowered, username));
        java.util.Arrays.fill(lowered, (char) 0);
        if (forbidden) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(
                    "password is too easy to guess; do not reuse a common word or the username");
        }
    }
```

Ship the deny list as a resource file so it can be refreshed without a code change, and test the
boundary cases already used for the collision guard so a `char[]`-based comparison never reintroduces
a `String` copy of the secret (see SEC-04).

## 6. Verified Controls and Checks With No Finding

- **Key stretching parameters** — `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256` at 210 000 iterations producing a 256-bit
  key (`PasswordHasher.java:22-26, 144-152`), roughly a third of a second per guess. This is at or
  above current guidance for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, so newly created records are not a CWE-916 finding;
  only the accepted-range floor is (SEC-03).
- **Salt generation and uniqueness** — `new SecureRandom()` (`PasswordHasher.java:33`) filling a fresh
  16-byte salt per account inside `hash` (`PasswordHasher.java:86-87`), never reused across accounts
  and never derived from the username or a timestamp, so identical passwords yield different records
  and precomputed tables do not apply.
- **Constant-time verification** — `MessageDigest.isEqual(expected, actual)`
  (`PasswordHasher.java:133`) rather than `Arrays.equals` or a `String.equals` loop, so verification
  time does not depend on how many digest bytes match.
- **Existence does not leak through login timing** — the unknown-user branch performs a real key
  derivation against fixed inputs (`AccountService.java:107-111`, `PasswordHasher.java:139-142`), so
  wrong-username and wrong-password attempts cost the same, and `AccountSystemTest` asserts the ratio
  stays within bounds. The login failure message is a single generic string for every failure
  (`Main.java:100-102`), so no CWE-204 response discrepancy exists on the login path.
- **Existence does not leak through registration timing either** — `PasswordHasher.hash(password)` is
  evaluated before the existence check inside `store.add(...)` (`AccountService.java:85`), so a
  duplicate-name attempt costs the same as a new registration; only the message distinguishes them
  (`Main.java:83`), which is inherent to any uniqueness-enforcing registry and is the documented
  trade-off.
- **Password-identity collisions closed** — trailing NULs and unpaired surrogates are refused rather
  than cleaned (`PasswordHasher.java:65-79`), which closes a real cross-account authentication
  collision in `PBEKeySpec`; `AccountSystemTest.rawDeriveBytes` proves the raw JCE really collapses
  those passwords before the program rejects them.
- **Username charset is an allowlist** — `[A-Za-z0-9._-]`, 3–32 characters
  (`AccountService.java:51-74`), with `trimSpacesOnly` (`AccountService.java:119-131`) instead of
  `String.trim()`. This blocks identity folding (`alice\n`, `alice\t`, `alice` + NUL, look-alike code
  points) *and* makes store-line forgery impossible: `|`, CR and LF can never reach
  `User.toLine()` (`User.java:20-24`), so the field separator cannot be injected.
- **Corrupt store fails closed** — a record with the wrong field count, a bad version, an
  unparseable timestamp, or a repeated username aborts the run with `IllegalStateException`
  (`User.java:29-40`, `AccountStore.java:130-139`); the program never half-loads a credential file to
  decide who may log in, and `PasswordHasher.matches` returns `false` for an unparseable record rather
  than throwing, so a caller cannot distinguish "no such account" from "damaged record"
  (`PasswordHasher.java:102-125`).
- **No lost-update or TOCTOU in registration** — `add` takes an exclusive `FileChannel` lock, re-reads
  the file *inside* the critical section, merges anything another process added, and replaces the file
  with `ATOMIC_MOVE` (`AccountStore.java:86-108, 145-171`); `load` takes a shared lock only for the
  snapshot (`AccountStore.java:57-68`). The duplicate check therefore reflects disk state, not the
  possibly stale in-memory map, and six racing processes were confirmed not to lose accounts.
- **Store and temp-file permissions are not permissive (disproved CWE-732 / CWE-377)** — the file is
  written via `Files.createTempFile(storeFile.getParent(), ...)`
  (`AccountStore.java:153`), which on POSIX creates the file with owner read/write only (`0600`)
  regardless of umask, and the replacement is a rename
  (`StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE`, `AccountStore.java:156`) that preserves those bits rather than
  inheriting the destination's permissions. The parent directory always exists because line 36
  absolutises the path, so the temp file is created beside the store rather than in a shared `/tmp`,
  and every failure path deletes it in a `finally` block (`AccountStore.java:162-170`). No finding.
- **Secret material destroyed after use** — `PBEKeySpec.clearPassword()` in a `finally` block
  (`PasswordHasher.java:150-152`), derived digests zeroed (`PasswordHasher.java:93, 135`), and caller
  buffers zeroed via `Arrays.fill` on every exit path including `System.exit` (`Main.java:86-87, 105,
  120`). The console path uses `Console.readPassword`, which returns a `char[]` and never creates a
  `String` (`Main.java:198-204`); only the piped fallback does (SEC-04).
- **Error messages do not leak internals** — `main` catches `IllegalArgumentException` and
  `IllegalStateException` and prints only `e.getMessage()` (`Main.java:55-61`), and every such message
  is a fixed, user-facing string written at the throw site; no stack trace, no class name, no file
  offset and no stored hash reaches stderr, and `IOException` causes are summarised without exposing
  parsing state (`AccountStore.java:47-49, 63-64, 103-104`).
- **Plaintext passwords are never persisted or reflected** — `User` holds only the self-describing
  encoding (`User.java:11`), `toLine` writes version, username, encoding and epoch second
  (`User.java:20-24`), and no output statement prints a password or a derived key; `list` reports a
  count and a path, never usernames (`Main.java:124-127`), so it is not an enumeration channel.
- **`run.sh` has no shell injection surface (checked against CWE-78)** — `set -u` is active, `PROJ_DIR`
  and every path expansion are double-quoted, arguments are forwarded as `"$@"`, there is no `eval`,
  and the only unquoted expansions are `find` results naming the project's own fixed `.java` files,
  which contain no spaces or glob characters (`run.sh:9, 24, 30-32, 36`). A compilation failure is
  detected and exits 2 rather than falling through to the stale classes (`run.sh:30-34`).
- **Shipped bytecode matches the reviewed sources** — `javap -p -constants` on `out/account/*.class`
  reports `ITERATIONS = 210000`, `MIN_ITERATIONS = 10000`, `MAX_ITERATIONS = 20000000`,
  `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256` and the same user-facing strings as `src/`, so `run.sh` executing prebuilt
  classes is not currently a divergence or a backdoor. The residual risk is procedural, not a code
  defect: the rebuild trigger at `run.sh:24` compares source mtimes against `out/account/Main.class`,
  so sources restored with older timestamps (a checkout, a `cp -p`) would run classes that do not
  correspond to them.
- **Absent attack surface confirmed** — no database or query construction (no SQL/NoSQL injection),
  no HTML/template rendering or unescaped response body (no XSS, no SSTI, no Open Redirect), no
  network I/O of any kind (no SSRF, no TLS/certificate handling, no SSRF-to-metadata), no
  `ObjectInputStream`/XML/JSON deserialisation of untrusted bytes, no `Runtime.exec` or subprocess, no
  JWT or cookie handling, no cryptographic key files, and no logging or telemetry that could carry a
  secret. `--store` is a path the operator supplies directly to their own process, so there is no
  lower-privilege caller whose input could be composed into it (no path traversal).
- **No embedded credentials (checked against CWE-798)** — the only credential-shaped constants are
  `EQUALIZING_PASSWORD` and `EQUALIZING_SALT` (`PasswordHasher.java:42-43`), fixed inputs whose sole
  purpose is to make the unknown-user branch cost a real derivation; they guard nothing and are not
  secrets, so they are deliberately not reported.
- **No authorisation boundary to test** — the program has one local operator, no sessions, roles or
  tenants, and no cross-user data; broken-access-control and session-management findings are not
  applicable, and case-sensitive usernames (`Alice` ≠ `alice`) is a documented design choice rather
  than an access-control defect.


---

### 44) results-cyber/qwen/qwen/set_a/sallie/4/security/security_review.md

# Security Review: Account Registrar and Authenticator (Java)

## 1. Executive Summary

This is a dependency-free Java command-line program that registers a username/password pair,
stores only a PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 verifier in a flat file, and authenticates later against that
file. The core password-storage design is genuinely sound: per-account 16-byte `SecureRandom`
salt, a one-way salted derivation, `MessageDigest.isEqual` for comparison, key-derivation work
spent on every refusal so that timing does not leak whether an account exists, `char[]`
passwords that are wiped, and a store that refuses malformed records on load. 127 self-tests and
an 18-mutant mutation battery back those claims.

Ten findings remain, none of which is a broken hash. The two most consequential are outside the
crypto entirely: the program accepts a password as a **command-line argument**, which publishes
the secret to every local process through `ps` / `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` and into shell history
(SEC-01), and `login()` performs **no attempt counting, lockout, or rate limiting** of any kind,
so the ~85 ms derivation is the only thing between an attacker and an unbounded online guessing
rate (SEC-02). A cluster of medium findings covers the KDF work factor sitting roughly half of
the current OWASP recommendation while `tryParse` still accepts records as thin as 1,000 rounds
(SEC-03), a password policy that admits `Password1`-class secrets (SEC-04), file-permission
narrowing that fails **silently** (SEC-05), an unsynchronised whole-file rewrite that loses
updates and admits a registration TOCTOU (SEC-06), and credential material printed to stdout
(SEC-07). Lower-severity items are user enumeration through the non-timing channel that the
timing equalisation leaves open (SEC-08), a never-wiped filler array (SEC-09), and an
unvalidated `--store` / `ACCOUNT_STORE` path (SEC-10).

The README is candid about most of this — it lists rate limiting, lockout and concurrency safety
as "deliberately absent". That reduces surprise, not risk: this is reviewed as code, and each
documented gap is still reported below with a fix.

## 2. Scope

| Path | Lines | Role | Reviewed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `src/UserAccountApp.java` | 172 | CLI entry point: `register`, `login`, `inspect`, `selftest`, password acquisition, store path | Yes — full |
| `src/UserAccountService.java` | 93 | Registration and authentication rules, refusal statuses | Yes — full |
| `src/PasswordHasher.java` | 167 | PBKDF2 derivation, stored format, `verify`, `burnWork`, record parsing | Yes — full |
| `src/AccountStore.java` | 149 | Flat-file store: load/validate, add, atomic save, POSIX permissions | Yes — full |
| `src/Passwords.java` | 80 | Length bounds, unhashable-character guard, strength rule, wipe | Yes — full |
| `src/Usernames.java` | 54 | Username allowlist, space-only trim, `Locale.ROOT` fold | Yes — full |
| `src/SelfTest.java` | 676 | 127 behavioural checks; also reads `src/PasswordHasher.java` structurally | Yes — full (test code) |
| `README.md` | 175 | Design rationale; documents the argv usage examples and the absent controls | Yes — as evidence |
| `mutation-battery.sh` | 172 | 18 targeted defects, each required to be caught | Yes — informational only |
| `out/*.class` | 12 files | Compiled output of `src/` | No — derived artefacts, not source |
| `prompt.txt`, `cyber_prompt.txt`, `prompt_hash.txt`, `return.txt`, `result.md` | — | Harness/review metadata, not product code | No — out of scope |
| `security_review.md` | — | This report | — |

No deserialisation sink, no network listener, no session or token issuance, and no privilege
boundary crossing exist in this codebase, which bounds the applicable vulnerability classes.

## 3. Skills Applied

Selected by matching this program's behaviour against each skill's description, then applied one
at a time with `file:line` citations.

1. **`review-code-for-security-vulnerabilities`** — the dispatcher: understand all code first,
   match skills, apply bodies, report with CWE + `file:line` + fix.
2. **`performing-cryptographic-audit-of-application`** — drove SEC-03 and SEC-09, and the audit
   of primitive choice, salt generation/length, KDF work factor, comparison semantics, and
   secret lifetime. Its "weak KDF / low-iteration PBKDF2" row and its pointer to the OWASP
   Password Storage Cheat Sheet are the basis for the iteration-count finding; the recommended
   figure (600,000 for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256) was taken from that cheat sheet rather than from
   memory.
3. **`testing-api-authentication-weaknesses`** — OWASP API2:2023. Step 6 supplied the two checks
   that produced SEC-04 (weak-policy acceptance: the skill's own example list includes
   `Password1`, "meets basic complexity but is common") and SEC-08 (account enumeration by
   comparing the response for a valid versus an invalid account). Steps 1–5 (JWT, token
   lifecycle, unauthenticated endpoint discovery) have **no applicable surface** here — this
   program issues no tokens, sessions, or cookies — and are recorded in §6 as checked-with-no-
   finding.
4. **`performing-hash-cracking-with-hashcat`** — quantified the offline cost of a stolen store
   for SEC-03 and SEC-04, and supplied the validation criterion that matters here: a rule-based
   attack that "cracks policy-compliant passwords", which is exactly what a
   `length + two character classes` policy produces. Note that PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 is hashcat
   mode 10000; that mode is not listed in the skill's hash-type table, so the mapping comes from
   general knowledge.
5. **`exploiting-race-condition-vulnerabilities`** — TOCTOU / limit-overrun framing for SEC-06.
   The skill's scenario 5, "Account Registration Bypass — create multiple accounts with the same
   email by submitting concurrent registration requests", is the exact shape of
   `AccountStore.add`'s check-then-write.

**Reviewed and recorded as having no applicable sink:** `exploiting-insecure-deserialization`.
That skill's triggers are Java `ObjectInputStream` (`aced0005` / `rO0AB`), PHP `O:`, .NET
ViewState, Python `pickle`, and YAML `!!python/object`. None is present: the store is parsed by
hand with `line.indexOf('\t')` and `split("\\$", -1)`, then validated field by field
(`PasswordHasher.java:112-141`). See §6.

**Behaviours checked against general OWASP/CWE knowledge with no matching skill in the library:**
secrets exposed through process argv (CWE-214, SEC-01); filesystem permission assignment and
silent failure (CWE-276/732, SEC-05); credential material written to stdout and therefore into
logs and scrollback (CWE-532/212, SEC-07); symlink/path handling of the `--store` and
`ACCOUNT_STORE` inputs (CWE-59/377, SEC-10); memory wiping of residual secret material
(CWE-226, SEC-09, cross-checked against the cryptographic-audit skill).

## 4. Summary of Findings

| ID | Severity | CWE | Title | Location |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SEC-01 | High | CWE-214, CWE-522 | Password accepted as a command-line argument | `src/UserAccountApp.java:114-116` |
| SEC-02 | High | CWE-307 | No attempt limit, lockout, or rate limiting on login | `src/UserAccountService.java:60-76` |
| SEC-03 | Medium | CWE-916, CWE-326 | PBKDF2 work factor below current guidance; 1,000-round records still accepted | `src/PasswordHasher.java:21-23, 126` |
| SEC-04 | Medium | CWE-521 | Password policy admits common single-pattern secrets | `src/Passwords.java:4, 52-72` |
| SEC-05 | Medium | CWE-276, CWE-732 | Store permission narrowing fails silently | `src/AccountStore.java:127-135` |
| SEC-06 | Medium | CWE-362, CWE-367 | Unlocked whole-file read-modify-write; registration TOCTOU | `src/AccountStore.java:32-62, 80-89, 93-125` |
| SEC-07 | Medium | CWE-532, CWE-212 | Verifier material printed to stdout | `src/UserAccountApp.java:61-62, 104-110` |
| SEC-08 | Low | CWE-204 | Account enumeration through the non-timing channel | `src/UserAccountService.java:64, 68, 73, 79-81, 89-92`, `src/UserAccountApp.java:72, 100` |
| SEC-09 | Low | CWE-226 | Derivation filler array is never wiped | `src/PasswordHasher.java:35-36, 89-98` |
| SEC-10 | Low | CWE-59, CWE-377 | Unvalidated account-store path from argv or environment | `src/UserAccountApp.java:136-143` |

## 5. Detailed Findings

### SEC-01 — Password accepted as a command-line argument

**Severity:** High
**CWE:** CWE-214 (Sensitive Information in Process Arguments), CWE-522 (Insufficiently Protected Credentials)
**Location:** `src/UserAccountApp.java:114-116`; reached from `:55` (`register`) and `:83` (`login`); examples at `README.md:118, 120`

**Vulnerable code**

```java
    private static char[] takePassword(String[] args, int index, String prompt) {
        if (args.length > index && !"-".equals(args[index])) {
            return args[index].toCharArray();
        }
        Console console = System.console();
```

`README.md:118` and `README.md:120` present this as the primary usage:

```bash
java -cp out UserAccountApp register AdaLovelace 'Correct Horse 9'
java -cp out UserAccountApp login    adalovelace 'Correct Horse 9'
```

**Why it is a problem**

Everything after `java` in that line is stored verbatim in the process's argument vector, which
on Linux is world-readable through `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` and is rendered by `ps aux`, `top`,
`htop`, `ps -ef` in `auditd`/`syslog` process-accounting records, monitoring agents, crash
reporters, and shell history (`.bash_history` keeps the whole line, quotes and all). The secret
therefore outlives the process immediately, is copied into every log and terminal recording of
the invocation, and cannot be revoked from those copies. It also defeats the care taken
everywhere else in this program: the password is carefully carried as `char[]` and wiped
(`UserAccountApp.java:57, 85`, `Passwords.java:75-79`), yet it arrives through a channel that is
more exposed than the verifier file it protects. A `Console` prompt path and a `-` stdin path
already exist (`UserAccountApp.java:118-131`), so the argv form buys nothing except exposure.

**Fix**

Never read a secret from argv. Keep the prompt path, keep `-` for "read from standard input", and
refuse a literal password argument with a message that says why:

```java
    private static char[] takePassword(String[] args, int index, String prompt) {
        if (args.length > index && !"-".equals(args[index])) {
            System.err.println("Refusing a password given as an argument: command lines are visible"
                    + " to every local process (ps, /proc/<pid>/cmdline) and are kept in shell"
                    + " history. Omit the argument to be prompted, or pass '-' to read it from stdin.");
            System.exit(2);
            return new char[0];
        }
        Console console = System.console();
        // ... unchanged prompt / stdin paths ...
    }
```

Update `README.md:110-122` so the documented examples are the safe ones. Note that the
`positional()` helper at `UserAccountApp.java:147` already drops option-looking tokens, so
dropping the argv password does not disturb option parsing. For genuinely non-interactive use,
read from a mode-0600 file descriptor (`--password-file` opened and wiped) rather than argv.


### SEC-02 — No attempt limit, lockout, or rate limiting on login

**Severity:** High
**CWE:** CWE-307 (Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts)
**Location:** `src/UserAccountService.java:60-76`; absence acknowledged at `README.md:169-172`

**Vulnerable code**

```java
    public Outcome login(String rawUsername, char[] candidate) {
        String username = Usernames.normalize(rawUsername);
        if (username == null || !Passwords.withinLength(candidate)) {
            hasher.burnWork();
            return new Outcome(username == null ? Status.INVALID_USERNAME : Status.INVALID_PASSWORD);
        }
        if (!Passwords.isHashable(candidate)) {
            hasher.burnWork();
            return new Outcome(Status.REJECTED);
        }
        Optional<String> stored = store.verifierFor(username);
        if (stored.isEmpty()) {
            hasher.burnWork();
            return new Outcome(Status.REJECTED);
        }
        boolean matched = hasher.verify(candidate, stored.get());
        return new Outcome(matched ? Status.OK : Status.REJECTED);
    }
```

**Why it is a problem**

`UserAccountService` keeps no state between calls (`:26-27` are the only fields), so nothing in
the authentication path counts attempts, remembers failures, delays repeats, or locks an account.
`README.md:169-170` lists "rate limiting and lockout after repeated failures" as deliberately
absent, which is a statement of scope rather than a mitigation: the class is written as a
reusable service — it takes `char[]` candidates and returns a structured `Outcome` — and any
embedding that puts `login()` behind a socket, form handler, or automation endpoint inherits an
unbounded guessing oracle from it. Two consequences follow. First, online guessing is limited
only by the caller's CPU: nothing here even slows a scripted loop on the *same* account, and
credential stuffing across usernames is not considered at all. Second, the equalising
`burnWork()` at `:63, 67, 72` means an unauthenticated caller can force a full 310,000-round
derivation per request without holding any credential, so the same missing counter is also the
cheapest available CPU-exhaustion vector. The 310,000 rounds protect a *stolen file* (an offline
attacker pays per guess); they do not protect the *live endpoint*, where the defender pays per
guess on the attacker's schedule.

**Fix**

Add a failure counter keyed on the account (and, when exposed over a channel, on the source
identity), returning the same uniform refusal so the counter itself is not an oracle:

```java
    private static final int MAX_FAILURES = 10;
    private static final long COOLDOWN_NANOS = java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.MINUTES.toNanos(15);

    private final java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentMap<String, long[]> failures =
            new java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentMap<String, Long> lockedUntil =
            new java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public Outcome login(String rawUsername, char[] candidate) {
        String username = Usernames.normalize(rawUsername);
        if (username != null && isLockedOut(username)) {
            hasher.burnWork();                       // keep refusal cost identical
            return new Outcome(Status.REJECTED);
        }
        // ... existing shape checks, unchanged ...
        boolean matched = hasher.verify(candidate, stored.get());
        if (matched) {
            failures.remove(username);
            lockedUntil.remove(username);
        } else {
            noteFailure(username);
        }
        return new Outcome(matched ? Status.OK : Status.REJECTED);
    }

    private boolean isLockedOut(String username) {
        Long until = lockedUntil.get(username);
        return until != null && System.nanoTime() < until;
    }

    private void noteFailure(String username) {
        long[] state = failures.compute(username, (key, previous) -> {
            long now = System.nanoTime();
            if (previous == null || now - previous[1] > COOLDOWN_NANOS) {
                return new long[] {1, now};
            }
            previous[0]++;
            return previous;
        });
        if (state[0] >= MAX_FAILURES) {
            lockedUntil.put(username, System.nanoTime() + COOLDOWN_NANOS);
            failures.remove(username);
        }
    }
```

For anything beyond a single process, the counters must live in shared storage (Redis, a DB
row) with both per-account and per-source keys, plus exponential backoff and an alert on the
threshold being reached — the same remediation the race-condition skill prescribes for
attempt-limiting mechanisms ("implement distributed locks for multi-server environments").


### SEC-03 — PBKDF2 work factor below current guidance, with a 1,000-round acceptance floor

**Severity:** Medium
**CWE:** CWE-916 (Use of Password Hash With Insufficient Computational Effort), CWE-326 (Inadequate Encryption Strength)
**Location:** `src/PasswordHasher.java:21-23`, enforced at `:126`, used at `:79`; no upgrade path (`README.md:171-172`)

**Vulnerable code**

```java
    public static final int DEFAULT_ITERATIONS = 310_000;
    public static final int MIN_ITERATIONS = 1_000;
    public static final int MAX_ITERATIONS = 5_000_000;
```

```java
        if (rounds < MIN_ITERATIONS || rounds > MAX_ITERATIONS) {
            return null;
        }
```

**Why it is a problem**

Two separate weaknesses share one constant block.

*The default is behind the times.* OWASP's Password Storage Cheat Sheet currently states
"PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256: 600,000 iterations (recommended)". `DEFAULT_ITERATIONS = 310_000` is about
half that, so a file disclosed today costs an attacker half the work the design intended. The
absence of re-hashing "when the round count is raised" (`README.md:171-172`) makes this strictly
worse over time: verifiers are written once at the creation-time cost and never revisited, so
every stored account is permanently marked with the hardware assumptions of the day it was
created, and raising the constant only helps accounts registered after the change.

*The acceptance floor is a policy hole.* `MIN_ITERATIONS = 1_000` is not a "legacy compatibility"
floor, it is 310 times cheaper than the policy. `tryParse` accepts any record in
[1,000, 5,000,000] and `verify` then derives using `record.iterations()` (`:79`), so the
attacker-relevant work factor is read from the same file an attacker wants to crack. A store
that was ever written by a lower setting — `SelfTest` legitimately builds temp stores at 2,000
rounds (`SelfTest.java:82, 258, 436`), and `PasswordHasher(int)` is public — is accepted silently
and forever by the default configuration; the program never warns that the accounts it is
protecting are up to 310x weaker than it claims in its own documentation. In cracking terms (the applied hash-cracking skill's
methodology), a 1,000-round PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 record is a fast-hash target: a dictionary plus
rules run against it at GPU wordlist rates, not at the "tens of thousands of times more expensive
per guess" rate that `README.md:30` promises.

There is a second-order effect on the program's headline control. `burnWork()` always derives at
the *hasher's* cost, while `verify` derives at the *record's* cost, so for a 1,000-round record a
wrong password returns in well under a millisecond while an unknown account returns in ~85 ms.
That is precisely the "instant for unknown users, slow for known ones" signal
`README.md:52-56` says the design exists to remove — reachable without any password at all.

**Fix**

Separate "parseable" from "allowed by policy", and make the cost a property of the deployment
rather than of the file:

```java
    public static final int DEFAULT_ITERATIONS = 600_000;   // OWASP: 600,000 for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256
    public static final int MIN_ITERATIONS = 1_000;         // parse floor: what the format can express
    public static final int MAX_ITERATIONS = 5_000_000;
    /** Records below this are refused outright: the file must not set the security level. */
    public static final int POLICY_MIN_ITERATIONS = DEFAULT_ITERATIONS;

    public static boolean meetsPolicy(StoredRecord record) {
        return record != null && record.iterations() >= POLICY_MIN_ITERATIONS;
    }
```

Refuse sub-policy records at load time rather than accepting them quietly
(`AccountStore.load`, around `:55`):

```java
            if (Usernames.normalize(user) == null
                    || PasswordHasher.tryParse(verifier) == null
                    || !PasswordHasher.meetsPolicy(PasswordHasher.tryParse(verifier))) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("Weak or malformed account store " + file
                        + " at line " + (i + 1));
            }
```

and upgrade on successful login so the cost can rise over the store's lifetime:

```java
        boolean matched = hasher.verify(candidate, stored.get());
        if (matched) {
            PasswordHasher.StoredRecord record = PasswordHasher.tryParse(stored.get());
            if (record.iterations() < hasher.iterations()) {
                store.replace(username, hasher.hash(candidate));   // same password, current cost
            }
        }
```

Measure the new default rather than trusting a constant: pick the highest round count that keeps
verification inside the latency budget on the deployed hardware, and document the measured value.
If the format can be changed, `README.md:173-175` is right that Argon2id (`m=19456, t=2, p=1`) or
scrypt (`N=2^17, r=8, p=1`) resist GPU and custom-hardware cracking far better than PBKDF2. Also
consider a pepper — a secret mixed into the derivation and held *apart* from the store file, which
is what makes a file disclosure alone insufficient.


### SEC-04 — Password policy admits common single-pattern secrets

**Severity:** Medium
**CWE:** CWE-521 (Weak Password Requirements)
**Location:** `src/Passwords.java:4`, `src/Passwords.java:52-72`; called from `src/UserAccountService.java:42-43`

**Vulnerable code**

```java
    public static boolean strongEnough(char[] password) {
        if (!withinLength(password)) {
            return false;
        }
        boolean lower = false;
        boolean upper = false;
        boolean digit = false;
        boolean other = false;
        for (char c : password) {
            if (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') {
                lower = true;
            } else if (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') {
                upper = true;
            } else if (c >= '0' && c <= '9') {
                digit = true;
            } else {
                other = true;
            }
        }
        int classes = (lower ? 1 : 0) + (upper ? 1 : 0) + (digit ? 1 : 0) + (other ? 1 : 0);
        return classes >= 2;
    }
```

**Why it is a problem**

The rule is `length >= 8` plus "at least two character classes", with no denylist and no
comparison against breached or common passwords. Every example the applied authentication skill
uses to demonstrate a weak policy is accepted here: `Password1`, `passw0rd`, `qwerty123`,
`abcABC123`, `letmein1`. Character-class counting is a 2005-era proxy that does not measure
guessability at all — it rewards exactly the capitalise-first-letter, append-a-digit,
substitute-a-zero transformations that hashcat's `best64`-style rule sets exist to generate.
Because this program's entire defence against a disclosed store is "the password was not
guessable" (`README.md:32-33` says as much: "no stored password is *literally* unrecoverable,
because people choose guessable passwords"), the policy is not a UX detail; it is the term that
multiplies the KDF cost from SEC-03. A single cracked common password in the file is a full
account takeover regardless of how many rounds were used. The README's own demo secret,
`'Correct Horse 9'` (`README.md:118`), is a dictionary-phrase pattern of exactly this class.

**Fix**

Set a length floor of 12, relax the composition requirement only for genuinely long passphrases,
and reject known-breached values. The comparison must not materialise the password as a `String`,
which would defeat the `char[]` discipline used elsewhere:

```java
    public static final int MIN_LENGTH = 12;
    private static final String[] DENIED = {
        "password", "password1", "passw0rd", "qwerty123", "12345678", "iloveyou", "letmein1",
    };

    public static boolean strongEnough(char[] password) {
        if (!withinLength(password)) {
            return false;
        }
        if (password.length < 12 && characterClasses(password) < 3) {
            return false;                       // short secrets must be mixed; long ones may not
        }
        char[] folded = new char[password.length];
        try {
            for (int i = 0; i < password.length; i++) {
                folded[i] = Character.toLowerCase(password[i]);
            }
            for (String denied : DENIED) {
                if (matchesIgnoringCase(folded, denied)) {
                    return false;
                }
            }
            return true;
        } finally {
            java.util.Arrays.fill(folded, '\0');
        }
    }

    private static boolean matchesIgnoringCase(char[] folded, String denied) {
        if (folded.length != denied.length()) {
            return false;
        }
        for (int i = 0; i < denied.length(); i++) {
            if (folded[i] != Character.toLowerCase(denied.charAt(i))) {
                return false;
            }
        }
        return true;
    }
```

A static list is the floor, not the answer. For real coverage check the candidate against a
breached-password corpus using a k-anonymised range query, and measure the resulting entropy
against the store's own cracking cost rather than against a class count.


### SEC-05 — Permission narrowing fails silently

**Severity:** Medium
**CWE:** CWE-276 (Incorrect Default Permissions), CWE-732 (Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource)
**Location:** `src/AccountStore.java:127-135`, called at `:106` and `:113`; no mode check in `load()` at `:32-62`

**Vulnerable code**

```java
    private static void narrowPermissions(Path path) {
        try {
            Set<PosixFilePermission> only = Set.of(
                    PosixFilePermission.OWNER_READ, PosixFilePermission.OWNER_WRITE);
            Files.setPosixFilePermissions(path, only);
        } catch (UnsupportedOperationException | IOException e) {
            // Filesystem without POSIX permissions, or the file vanished: nothing else to do.
        }
    }
```

**Why it is a problem**

The file being protected is the credential store, and this is the only line of defence applied to
it. The catch is total: `UnsupportedOperationException` means the filesystem has no POSIX
permissions at all — the case where the protection is entirely absent — and the program
continues, prints nothing, and exits `0` as if the store were protected. `IOException` is treated
the same way. So on Windows NTFS, on SMB/CIFS and NFS mounts, inside some container bind mounts,
and on any filesystem where the `chmod` fails, the store's accessibility is decided by directory
ACL inheritance and the mount's permission masks with no signal to the operator, while
`README.md:83` states flatly that "the file is set to `0600` (only the owner may read it)".
Three specific gaps follow. (1) No verification: the code never reads back the attributes it
believes it applied. (2) No operator feedback: a protection that silently did not happen is worse
than one that fails loudly, because it removes the reason to look. (3) No check of an
*already-existing* file: `load()` inspects every byte of the store's *content* for malformed
records (`:44-59`) but never asks who can read the file, so a store created world-readable by
`cp`, `scp`, a shared-directory umask, or a restore from backup keeps working for years while
being open to every local account. Note the one mitigating fact, so this is not overstated:
`Files.createTempFile` creates the temp file owner-only on POSIX, and `ATOMIC_MOVE` preserves that
inode's mode, so the normal Linux save path does yield `0600` even if the `chmod` at `:113`
failed — which is exactly why a silent catch is easy to ship and hard to notice.

**Fix**

Verify what was applied, and make the unprotectable case loud rather than invisible:

